articles.title: A Major Reform of California's Environmental Regulations Looks Destined for Failure
articles.content:
Official results have yet to be called, but California's Proposition 45, which would have dramatically scaled back environmental review requirements for everything from new energy infrastructure to new highways, is looking set for defeat.
With an estimated 65 percent of the vote counted, Proposition 45 is trailing with 45.1 percent of votes in favor and 54.9 percent of votes opposed.
That's a massive and growing gulf that the measure does not seem likely to overcome.
Should Proposition 45 go down, it will be a major setback for the movement to make California a state that builds.
The target of the measure's reforms is the California Environmental Quality Act, which requires government agencies to study the environmental impacts of public projects they undertake directly as well as private projects they have some discretionary control over.
In practice, that means everything from a new publicly sponsored highway to a privately built suburban subdivision must be studied for its effects on noise, air quality, traffic, archaeological resources, and more.
Additionally, the law empowers third parties to challenge agency approvals of projects in court by asserting that this or that environmental impact was not studied thoroughly enough.
These features have made CEQA notorious for slowing down development in the Golden State. The most stringent levels of CEQA review can take years. For some major projects, the environmental study phase can stretch out for decades.
The law has also become project opponents' weapon of choice for slowing down disfavored projects. Everyone from labor unions to rival developers has also used the threat of CEQA litigation to extract concessions from project sponsors.
These problems haven't gone unrecognized in California. Former Gov. Jerry Brown called CEQA reform "the Lord's work." Current Gov. Gavin Newsom has criticized the law for stopping development (although he declined to endorse Proposition 45).
In fits and starts, the Legislature has exempted whole categories of projects (most significantly, urban infill housing) from CEQA reform.
Proposition 45 was an ambitious effort initiated by the state's Chamber of Commerce to reform core elements of the law for a much broader array of projects.
It would have created an opt-in streamlined CEQA process for "essential" projects, including everything from energy and water infrastructure to highways to suburban housing and more.
This streamlined process would be governed by binding shot clocks. The most stringent forms of CEQA review would have to be completed within a year, for instance. Rather than consider an indeterminate number of environmental impacts, this streamlined process would only require project sponsors to confirm that their project complied with objective, quantifiable existing regulations.
The initiative would also have narrowed the grounds on which project opponents could sue under CEQA. CEQA lawsuits would also have to be decided on an expedited schedule.
Proponents of Proposition 45 pitched their proposition as less radical than the long list of CEQA exceptions that had been passed by the Legislature. The initiative didn't guarantee any project would get approved. It didn't allow any projects to fully skip CEQA review.
Nevertheless, there was no getting around the fact that the streamlined opt-in process was far different, and far less rigorous, than what CEQA requires today.
It thus attracted widespread opposition from environmental groups, unions, and Jane Fonda. It also split pro-housing groups who've long supported reforming CEQA to make urban housing and transportation development easier.
Some of these groups opposed the measure because it would enable more single-family greenfield development. Some of the state's biggest YIMBY ("yes in my backyard") organizations declined to either endorse or oppose it.
Putting ambitious CEQA reform on the ballot was an untested proposition. As the votes come in, Proposition 45 is increasingly looking like a failed proposition.
There are a few takeaways from the initiative's probable failure. The first is that there really doesn't seem to be a coherent "abundance" movement. Not all groups that want more apartments want more single-family homes. Many of the people who are frustrated when CEQA stops new bike lanes are still happy to see the law block a highway.
When "build more of everything more quickly" was on the ballot, selective supporters of new development sided with the anti-growth forces. And that's enough for a majority to take down Proposition 45.
The second takeaway is that, in California at least, the voters don't see broad-based permitting reform as a cure for widespread anger at rising costs of living.
Poll after poll showed that the midterm electorate was primarily motivated by high and rising prices and government corruption. Despite Proposition 45's proponents' best efforts to sell their permitting reform as an affordability measure, a majority of voters didn't buy it.
That all suggests some hard political limits on the political viability of a broad "abundance agenda," even if it is the correct policy.
On CEQA specifically, reform advocates will likely have to go back to their old tactics of pushing for specific exemptions and more modest reforms within the state Legislature.
The post A Major Reform of California's Environmental Regulations Looks Destined for Failure appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: As Chief of Staff, Stephen Miller Will Reinforce Trump's Worst Instincts
articles.content:
President Donald Trump today announced that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. That change does not bode well for anyone who hoped that Trump, chastened by his party's disastrous performance in the midterm elections, would moderate the policies that alienated voters.
Miller, previously a deputy chief of staff, is the main architect of Trump's immigration crackdown, which has targeted many peaceful and productive U.S. residents, contrary to the promise that it would focus on "the worst of the worst." Although Trump has intermittently expressed qualms about the impact of immigration enforcement on businesses and their longtime employees, Miller has made it clear that he favors an indiscriminate approach.
A January 2026 profile of Miller in The Atlantic described an exchange that epitomizes his attitude toward immigration. "Stephen, if you had it your way, everyone would look exactly like you," Trump reportedly told Miller, who was arguing about immigration policy with another White House aide. "That's correct," Miller replied.
Since illegal immigration is an "invasion," Miller told reporters in May 2025, the Trump administration was "actively looking" at suspending the writ of habeas corpus to facilitate its mass deportation campaign. "A lot of it depends on whether the courts do the right thing or not," he said. It turned out that Miller was not just spitballing: The New York Times later reported that his comment reflected a serious internal debate about whether to unilaterally override the ancient principle that people nabbed by the government have a right to challenge their detention in court.
Miller's support for aggressive immigration enforcement extends to violence against Americans who object to it. After immigration agents fatally shot Minneapolis protester Alex Pretti in January, Miller defied the video evidence by condemning him as "a domestic terrorist" and "would-be assassin" who "tried to murder federal law enforcement."
Last April, Miller described birthright citizenship as "the gravest and most preposterous of all constitutional abominations." Two months later, after the Supreme Court rejected Trump's attempt to rewrite the 14th Amendment, Miller called it "one of the most destructive and outrageous decisions" in the Court's history.
Miller also was appalled by judicial pushback against Trump's "emergency" tariffs. After the U.S. Court of International Trade rejected them in May 2025, he implied that it had no legitimate role in determining whether the president had the authority he claimed. "The judicial coup is out of control," he wrote on X. Last February, when the Supreme Court agreed that Trump's tariffs were illegal, Miller condemned the decision as "cowardly" and "horrendous," saying the justices were "torturing" the law and the Constitution.
Miller's hostility toward judicial review mirrors Trump's attitude. Also like Trump, Miller has no compunctions about punishing people for constitutionally protected speech.
In November 2023, after Media Matters for America reported that X was "placing ads for Apple, Bravo, IBM, Oracle, and Xfinity next to pro-Nazi content," Miller urged "conservative state Attorneys General" to investigate the organization for "fraud." Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey took Miller's advice, launching investigations that were ultimately blocked by federal courts on First Amendment grounds.
After conservative activist Charlie Kirk was assassinated in September 2025, Miller blamed a "vast domestic terror movement," including "messaging designed to trigger [and] incite violence"—i.e., harsh political rhetoric. "In Charlie's name," he said, "we are going to use every resource we have at the Department of Justice, Homeland Security, and throughout this government to identify, disrupt, dismantle, and destroy these networks."
Miller, in short, is apt to be the opposite of a calming influence on Trump. His elevation seems likely to reinforce the president's worst instincts.
The post As Chief of Staff, Stephen Miller Will Reinforce Trump's Worst Instincts appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: White House Warns Conservative Groups It Is 'Monitoring' What They Say Amid Discontent Over Midterm Results
articles.content:
With President Donald Trump's unpopularity front and center after Democrats' sweeping midterm victory, Republicans are beginning to criticize the president and his policies.
On Wednesday, Vice President J.D. Vance called out Trump's war of choice in Iran as the "real reason" for why the GOP lost the election. Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has spent the last few days dissecting voter dissatisfaction, which he told The Sage Steele Show includes the crony capitalism of the "Republicans in Washington." With the GOP seemingly fracturing, the White House is taking steps to rein in potential fallout within the base.
On Thursday, the White House Office of Public Liaison sent a memo to over 3,000 conservative organizations, which The Wall Street Journal reports, "laid out a list of Trump's accomplishments in office and pledged to prevent newly ascendant Democrats from reversing them." The memo ended with one sentence, highlighted in yellow: "As always, we are monitoring statements, press releases, and media engagements from your organizations."
When the Journal asked for comment, a White House spokeswoman said the memo "wasn't a threat and was part of a larger effort to mobilize outside supporters," insisting that the Office of Public Liaison has sent out similar messages in the past. The Journal didn't find similar language in a review of previous emails from the liaison's office to groups encouraging organizations' advocacy for the president.
It's certainly possible that the liaison office did not intend to threaten conservative groups—it is, after all, the job of the office to monitor what allied groups are doing. However, given the administration's history of tracking and threatening its critics for constitutionally protected speech, the line doesn't exactly read as a friendly reminder.
In September, for example, Trump banned several major news outlets from the White House, displeased with their negative reporting. "The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS." He stated on Truth Social. "It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!" A district court judge blocked the ban in October, finding that Trump's own words showed "unlawful viewpoint discrimination."
The Trump administration has also targeted legal residents for their political speech. Last year, Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested Mahmoud Khalil, a Columbia graduate student, over his role in pro-Palestine campus protests. Khalil was never charged with a crime. Still, the administration deemed he was "subject to removal" because his "presence or activities…would have potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States."
Trump isn't the first president to crack down on disfavored speech. During the COVID-19 pandemic, former President Joe Biden spent much of his time pressuring social media companies to remove content they deemed "misinformation." Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that Biden administration officials "repeatedly pressured our teams for months to censor certain COVID-19 content, including humor and satire."
If the Trump White House is threatening these groups, it's unclear what the consequences of disobeying might be. But one thing is for sure: With the president's popularity in doubt after the midterms, a memo reminding allies they're being watched suggests the White House fears its grip on the GOP is slipping.
The post White House Warns Conservative Groups It Is 'Monitoring' What They Say Amid Discontent Over Midterm Results appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Short Circuit: A roundup of recent federal court decisions
articles.content:
Please enjoy the latest edition of Short Circuit, a weekly feature written by a bunch of people at the Institute for Justice.
New on the Short Circuit podcast: We look at 100 years of zoning and chances of zoning reform, in court and in city councils, with Harvard's Molly Brady and Vice Mayor of Cambridge, Mass., Burhan Azeem.
And on the latest episode of the Law Office History podcast, Christian Burset of Penn Law explains how it was hard to be a textualist in Olde Timey England because Parliament wasn't very clear when writing its statutes and it was hard to find copies of them anyway.
- Sure, some observers would think that the interesting part of this First Circuit decision is the clash of parental rights in schools and a vaccine mandate of general applicability. (Despite recent SCOTUS decisions, no preliminary injunction will issue.) But, for us, the big news is that the First Circuit wrote an opinion in single-spaced Times New Roman. It's a start!
- Political group asks for a P.I. ahead of NYC's mayoral election, claiming it wants to run ads but that certain disclosure laws that apply to the ads are unconstitutional. The district court denied the motion and the group appealed. Second Circuit: The election was in, like, 2025. This is moot. You didn't say anything about the next election. Dissent: Actually, they did, especially if you look at the underlying complaint. Further, this disclosure regime is unconstitutional.
- Due to the evisceration of the Chevron doctrine the evisceration of the Administrative State continues. This time it's the Fourth Circuit eviscerating the . . . deportation of a Dominican woman working for an elder care provider who may have checked the wrong box on an employment form.
- District court sua sponteremands a removed case because the notice didn't adequately establish the plaintiffs' citizenship. Can the remand order be appealed? That depends, explains the Fifth Circuit, on whether the defect was jurisdictional or procedural. If jurisdictional, it can't be appealed no matter what. If procedural, it also can't if raised by a party. Since here it was raised sua sponte, though, the judge acted outside the statute, and that remand can be appealed.
- Ethiopian man slated for deportation to anywhere besides Ethiopia files a habeas petition six months after an immigration court deems him removable. When the gov't tries to put him on a flight to Cameroon (as it said it intended to do months earlier), he files emergency motions to prevent deportation. The district court denies his motions, but, while his appeal is pending, grants his habeas petition and orders his release into the U.S. Fifth Circuit (per curiam): Appeal dismissed as moot. None of this sits very well with Judge Oldham, whose statement respecting the dismissal describes the case as a "travesty" involving "gamesmanship," an "avalanche of self-contradicting gibberish," and a "magistrate judge's surprise switcheroo."
- Tabletop role-playing game aficionado develops a game designed to help people with anxiety and other psychological disorders. He enters into a licensing agreement with a company that promotes "geek therapy"—therapeutic techniques that incorporate geek culture. Things go south and the designer sues to company. The district court dismisses all his claims. Will he throw a saving roll on appeal? Fifth Circuit: Natural 1.
- Public employees in Indiana can have union dues deducted from their paychecks. Since 2021, teachers alone must take additional steps to do so, including signing a form that reads, "I am aware that I have a First Amendment right . . . to refrain from joining and paying dues to a union." A district court held that the statement was compelled speech in violation of . . . the First Amendment. So, Indiana amended it to "The State of Indiana wishes to make you aware . . . " Seventh Circuit: The rewrite resolves the compelled speech problem, but making teachers jump through additional hoops is viewpoint discrimination in violation of . . . the First Amendment. Affirmed.
- Missouri man is convicted of being a felon in possession. Eighth Circuit precedent bars his Second Amendment claims but what about a Fifth Amendment claim? After all, states have different laws, and it would be unfair to disarm someone whose previous criminal conduct might be a misdemeanor in a different state. Eighth Circuit: Well, you were convicted of selling crack, which is a felony in all 50 states.
- Idaho physician challenges state abortion ban as applied to situations where an abortion is necessary to prevent serious and lasting—but not life-threatening—harm to pregnant women. District court grants injunction and Idaho seeks a stay pending appeal. Ninth Circuit: Granted. Concurrence: I mean, c'mon. Dobbs resolved all this. Dissent: Roe recognized two abortion rights: one privacy-based and one health-based. Dobbs only rejected the former, and history and tradition support the latter.
- Boise State student and trans athlete Lindsay Hecox challenged Idaho's Fairness in Women's Sports Act, but when the Supreme Court took her case, she disclaimed any interest in playing collegiate sports covered by the law and suggested her case was moot. The Supreme Court disagreed because she was still an enrolled student, upheld the law, and remanded to the Ninth Circuit. Ninth Circuit: But now she has withdrawn from the school, so the case really is moot, despite her claims that she wishes to re-enroll.
- Facebook invokes terms-of-service violations to terminate a content creator's decade-old account with 25 million followers. Creator: Sure, our ads are "scammy" and "blatant clickbait," but Facebook breached its agreement in deleting our account. Ninth Circuit: Even assuming you have an enforceable contractual right, you're seeking to meddle with Facebook's publishing discretion, which Section 230 bars.
- Football fans obtained a multi-billion-dollar jury verdict against the NFL, arguing that its anticompetitive agreements made them pay inflated prices for Sunday Ticket. Zoinks! The district court rejected the verdict, excluding the fans' expert as unreliable and entering judgment as a matter of law for the NFL. Ninth Circuit: Reversed from the booth. Expert opinions aren't unfounded or unreliable merely because they're impeachable. (Your humble summarist would submit that the Denver Broncos are super.)
- In Bivens news, exactly three people can win under Bivens. The terrorist Abu Hamza (complaining of the conditions of his life imprisonment) is not one of those three people. Therefore, he cannot win under Bivens. Tenth Circuit: Yup.
- You might be tempted to read this Eleventh Circuit opinion because a customer used "Cash App" to see if they could get themselves some "Scooby Snacks." But you'll get more out of it for the drug dealer defendant's (unsuccessful) attempts to request a Franks hearing and exclude hearsay.
- And in en banc news, the Fourth Circuit will not review its decision upholding a P.I. that allows fired CIA employees, who worked in DEI-related positions, to pursue internal employment appeals.
- And in further en banc news, the Fifth Circuit will not initially be going en banc in an appeal concerning whether Congress has power under the Commerce Clause to ban machine guns. The vote almost went over the top, though, 9-8.
- And in additional en banc news, the Fifth Circuit will reconsider its decision that Trader Joe's committed an unfair labor practice when it fired someone the dissent called "the sort of employee who haunts the nightmares of HR managers everywhere."
- And in wild, yet now not that newsworthy, en banc news, on Monday the Ninth Circuit granted a stay of a district court's TRO against the federal gov't related to the gov't's demand that California and Washington segregate certain ballots. Then, later that day, the Ninth Circuit granted a motion for the case to go en banc. Then, on Tuesday, the Ninth Circuit (the eleven-judge en banc panel) reinstated the initial stay. The plaintiffs then asked for "full court rehearing en banc," i.e., that all 29 active circuit judges plus the senior judge on the initial panel hear the case. Ninth Circuit (still on Tuesday): Full en banc? We never go full en banc.
Protectionism alert! This week, IJ sent a letter to officials in Clewiston, Florida, warning that the city's food truck ordinance violates the Florida Constitution. Food trucks in Clewiston may only operate on Mondays and Tuesdays and must stay at least 200 feet away from any open restaurant unless that restaurant gives written permission. Those two days are not a coincidence. Mondays and Tuesdays are when most brick-and-mortar restaurants in Clewiston are closed, meaning the ordinance permits food trucks only when they are unlikely to compete with established businesses. The 200-foot buffer zone fulfills a similar protectionist function, giving existing restaurants veto power over whether a competitor can set up nearby.
The post Short Circuit: A roundup of recent federal court decisions appeared first on Reason Magazine.

  2. Political group asks for a P.I. ahead of NYC's mayoral election, claiming it wants to run ads but that certain disclosure laws that apply to the ads are unconstitutional. The district court denied the motion and the group appealed. Second Circuit: The election was in, like, 2025. This is moot. You didn't say anything about the next election. Dissent: Actually, they did, especially if you look at the underlying complaint. Further, this disclosure regime is unconstitutional.
  3. Due to the evisceration of the Chevron doctrine the evisceration of the Administrative State continues. This time it's the Fourth Circuit eviscerating the . . . deportation of a Dominican woman working for an elder care provider who may have checked the wrong box on an employment form.
  4. District court sua sponteremands a removed case because the notice didn't adequately establish the plaintiffs' citizenship. Can the remand order be appealed? That depends, explains the Fifth Circuit, on whether the defect was jurisdictional or procedural. If jurisdictional, it can't be appealed no matter what. If procedural, it also can't if raised by a party. Since here it was raised sua sponte, though, the judge acted outside the statute, and that remand can be appealed.
  5. Ethiopian man slated for deportation to anywhere besides Ethiopia files a habeas petition six months after an immigration court deems him removable. When the gov't tries to put him on a flight to Cameroon (as it said it intended to do months earlier), he files emergency motions to prevent deportation. The district court denies his motions, but, while his appeal is pending, grants his habeas petition and orders his release into the U.S. Fifth Circuit (per curiam): Appeal dismissed as moot. None of this sits very well with Judge Oldham, whose statement respecting the dismissal describes the case as a "travesty" involving "gamesmanship," an "avalanche of self-contradicting gibberish," and a "magistrate judge's surprise switcheroo."
  6. Tabletop role-playing game aficionado develops a game designed to help people with anxiety and other psychological disorders. He enters into a licensing agreement with a company that promotes "geek therapy"—therapeutic techniques that incorporate geek culture. Things go south and the designer sues to company. The district court dismisses all his claims. Will he throw a saving roll on appeal? Fifth Circuit: Natural 1.
  7. Public employees in Indiana can have union dues deducted from their paychecks. Since 2021, teachers alone must take additional steps to do so, including signing a form that reads, "I am aware that I have a First Amendment right . . . to refrain from joining and paying dues to a union." A district court held that the statement was compelled speech in violation of . . . the First Amendment. So, Indiana amended it to "The State of Indiana wishes to make you aware . . . " Seventh Circuit: The rewrite resolves the compelled speech problem, but making teachers jump through additional hoops is viewpoint discrimination in violation of . . . the First Amendment. Affirmed.
  8. Missouri man is convicted of being a felon in possession. Eighth Circuit precedent bars his Second Amendment claims but what about a Fifth Amendment claim? After all, states have different laws, and it would be unfair to disarm someone whose previous criminal conduct might be a misdemeanor in a different state. Eighth Circuit: Well, you were convicted of selling crack, which is a felony in all 50 states.
  9. Idaho physician challenges state abortion ban as applied to situations where an abortion is necessary to prevent serious and lasting—but not life-threatening—harm to pregnant women. District court grants injunction and Idaho seeks a stay pending appeal. Ninth Circuit: Granted. Concurrence: I mean, c'mon. Dobbs resolved all this. Dissent: Roe recognized two abortion rights: one privacy-based and one health-based. Dobbs only rejected the former, and history and tradition support the latter.
  10. Boise State student and trans athlete Lindsay Hecox challenged Idaho's Fairness in Women's Sports Act, but when the Supreme Court took her case, she disclaimed any interest in playing collegiate sports covered by the law and suggested her case was moot. The Supreme Court disagreed because she was still an enrolled student, upheld the law, and remanded to the Ninth Circuit. Ninth Circuit: But now she has withdrawn from the school, so the case really is moot, despite her claims that she wishes to re-enroll.
  11. Facebook invokes terms-of-service violations to terminate a content creator's decade-old account with 25 million followers. Creator: Sure, our ads are "scammy" and "blatant clickbait," but Facebook breached its agreement in deleting our account. Ninth Circuit: Even assuming you have an enforceable contractual right, you're seeking to meddle with Facebook's publishing discretion, which Section 230 bars.
  12. Football fans obtained a multi-billion-dollar jury verdict against the NFL, arguing that its anticompetitive agreements made them pay inflated prices for Sunday Ticket. Zoinks! The district court rejected the verdict, excluding the fans' expert as unreliable and entering judgment as a matter of law for the NFL. Ninth Circuit: Reversed from the booth. Expert opinions aren't unfounded or unreliable merely because they're impeachable. (Your humble summarist would submit that the Denver Broncos are super.)
  13. In Bivens news, exactly three people can win under Bivens. The terrorist Abu Hamza (complaining of the conditions of his life imprisonment) is not one of those three people. Therefore, he cannot win under Bivens. Tenth Circuit: Yup.
  14. You might be tempted to read this Eleventh Circuit opinion because a customer used "Cash App" to see if they could get themselves some "Scooby Snacks." But you'll get more out of it for the drug dealer defendant's (unsuccessful) attempts to request a Franks hearing and exclude hearsay.
  15. And in en banc news, the Fourth Circuit will not review its decision upholding a P.I. that allows fired CIA employees, who worked in DEI-related positions, to pursue internal employment appeals.
  16. And in further en banc news, the Fifth Circuit will not initially be going en banc in an appeal concerning whether Congress has power under the Commerce Clause to ban machine guns. The vote almost went over the top, though, 9-8.
  17. And in additional en banc news, the Fifth Circuit will reconsider its decision that Trader Joe's committed an unfair labor practice when it fired someone the dissent called "the sort of employee who haunts the nightmares of HR managers everywhere."
  18. And in wild, yet now not that newsworthy, en banc news, on Monday the Ninth Circuit granted a stay of a district court's TRO against the federal gov't related to the gov't's demand that California and Washington segregate certain ballots. Then, later that day, the Ninth Circuit granted a motion for the case to go en banc. Then, on Tuesday, the Ninth Circuit (the eleven-judge en banc panel) reinstated the initial stay. The plaintiffs then asked for "full court rehearing en banc," i.e., that all 29 active circuit judges plus the senior judge on the initial panel hear the case. Ninth Circuit (still on Tuesday): Full en banc? We never go full en banc.

Protectionism alert! This week, IJ sent a letter to officials in Clewiston, Florida, warning that the city's food truck ordinance violates the Florida Constitution. Food trucks in Clewiston may only operate on Mondays and Tuesdays and must stay at least 200 feet away from any open restaurant unless that restaurant gives written permission. Those two days are not a coincidence. Mondays and Tuesdays are when most brick-and-mortar restaurants in Clewiston are closed, meaning the ordinance permits food trucks only when they are unlikely to compete with established businesses. The 200-foot buffer zone fulfills a similar protectionist function, giving existing restaurants veto power over whether a competitor can set up nearby.
